papers.title: Sustained Viral Suppression and its association with Psychiatric Morbidity and Sleep Quality among Older Adults with Human Immunodeficiency Virus: Evidence from a Retrospective Cohort in Ibadan, Nigeria.
papers.abstract: PurposeOlder adults with HIV are at risk of psychiatric disorders and poor sleep quality, but evidence from sub-Saharan Africa is limited, particularly regarding sustained viral suppression. This study examined the prevalence of psychiatric disorders and poor sleep quality symptoms and their association with sustained viral suppression among older adults with HIV in Nigeria. MethodsA retrospective cohort study was conducted among older adults receiving care at a tertiary HIV clinic in Ibadan, Nigeria. Viral load data from 2019-2023 were abstracted from medical records to determine sustained viral load suppression, while psychiatric morbidity and sleep quality were assessed cross-sectionally in 2023. Psychiatric assessments included major depressive disorder, anxiety disorder, bipolar disorder and mania. Mixed-effects logistic regression assessed changes in viral suppression over time and associations with psychiatric morbidity and sleep quality. ResultsAmong 400 participants, 63.5% were female and mean age was 58.2 years ({+/-} 6.5). A total of 25.8% had major depressive disorder, 17.5% had anxiety disorder, 29.3% had poor sleep quality, 3.3%, bipolar disorder, and 1.0% mania. Viral suppression improved significantly over the retrospective period. Sustained viral suppression was significantly associated with higher odds of good sleep quality (OR = 1.69, 95% CI: 1.07-2.66, p = 0.025), but not psychiatric morbidity. ConclusionPsychiatric disorders and poor sleep quality are common among older adults with HIV in Nigeria. Sustained viral suppression was associated with better sleep quality but not psychiatric morbidity highlighting the importance of integrating mental health and sleep assessment into comprehensive HIV care for older adults.

papers.title: TALQ: A reproducible language model questionnaire for dense measurement of depressive and anxious states
papers.abstract: Depression and anxiety are often assessed weeks or months apart with brief questionnaires covering few symptoms, leaving changes between assessments unobserved. Here, we introduce TALQ, a scoring system in which a large language model rates 52 symptoms from text, and use it to score 491 members of two online mental health communities every two weeks for a year. Ratings were stable across samples, predicted human annotations of interpersonal risk factors, low self-esteem and depression severity, and agreed with inventories completed by the same model. The scores mapped into 12 replicable symptom factors, including fearful preoccupation and social strain. Sleep disturbance and self-harm content consistently preceded overwhelm and emotional pain, respectively, two weeks later. People differed mainly in the states they occupied rather than transitions between them, and 13% entered in a crisis that remitted over months. Overall, our findings suggest that TALQ can measure expressed mental states densely and quantify longitudinal dynamics.

papers.title: Wearable-based sleep and activity tracking detects Parkinson's disease and associated pathological hallmarks
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is associated with sleep and motor function impairment, even in the early stages. Here, we investigated whether passive wearable-based sleep and activity tracking can detect PD and its associated pathological hallmarks, dopaminergic deficit and -synuclein pathology. Sleep and activity metrics (SAM) were derived from free-living wrist accelerometry data of a U.S. cohort and used to train a machine learning model (SAM-PD) to distinguish persons with PD (n = 133) from healthy controls (n = 26). The model achieved an AUROC of 0.93 and an AUPRC of 0.98, demonstrated excellent test-retest reliability, and generalized without retraining to an independent European cohort (n = 40; 50% PwPD) monitored with a different device (AUROC, 0.95; AUPRC, 0.95). REM sleep duration, walking cadence, and low-level acceleration features were most predictive. Applied to a U.S. at-risk cohort, SAM-PD performed comparably to the resource-intensive Movement Disorder Society (MDS) prodromal PD risk score in detecting dopaminergic deficit (AUROC, 0.86 vs. 0.80; AUPRC, 0.45 vs. 0.46; n = 121; 12.4% prevalence) and -synuclein pathology (AUROC, 0.76 for both; AUPRC 0.50 vs. 0.42; n = 114; 16.7% prevalence). A combination with the MDS score modestly improved detection. Findings support further evaluation of wearable monitoring for PD screening and biomarker enrichment in larger populations.

papers.title: Sleep Irregularity and Risk of Incident Hypertension in the UK Biobank
papers.abstract: Background: Irregular sleep patterns are common and have been associated with higher cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. Hypertension is the leading modifiable cause of CVD, but evidence linking irregular sleep to hypertension is inconsistent. The objective of this study was to quantify associations between irregular sleep and incident hypertension. Methods: We conducted a prospective cohort study among 55,572 UK Biobank participants without hypertension or anti-hypertensive medication use who provided 5 valid days of accelerometry in 2013-2015 (60% women, mean age 61 years). We measured sleep regularity using the intra-individual standard deviation (SD) of sleep duration and the sleep regularity index (SRI), a measure of the similarity of sleep-wake patterns from one day to the next. Cox proportional hazards models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (HR) for incident hypertension, identified through linked health records, by levels of sleep regularity adjusting for demographic, socioeconomic, and lifestyle factors as well as employment schedule. We also evaluated differences by demographic, clinical, and sleep-related (defined by duration, efficiency, timing, and sleep disorders) subgroups, and interaction with genetic susceptibility to hypertension. Results: During 7.9 years of follow-up, 5,713 participants developed hypertension. Participants with sleep duration SD >90 minutes had an 18% higher risk of incident hypertension compared to those with sleep duration SD 30 minutes (HR: 1.18; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.06, 1.31). Similarly, participants in the lowest SRI quintile had a 40% higher risk than those in the highest SRI quintile (HR: 1.40; 95% CI: 1.29, 1.52). These associations were generally consistent across demographic, health, and sleep-defined subgroups. Sleep irregularity and genetic susceptibility contributed independently to hypertension risk, without evidence of interaction. Conclusions: Irregular sleep patterns were associated with higher incident hypertension risk independent of established risk factors and genetic susceptibility. Maintaining regular sleep schedules may represent a modifiable behavioral target for hypertension prevention.

papers.title: EEG-Derived Proxies of Cortical Excitability in Epilepsy: Group Discrimination, Temporal Stability and Medication Sensitivity
papers.abstract: Objective To identify EEG-derived markers of cortical excitability that best distinguish people with epilepsy from healthy controls while maintaining stability across repeated recordings, and to assess the influence of antiseizure medication (ASM) burden on these measures. Methods Scalp EEG recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Epilepsy Corpus were analyzed, including 1,404 recordings from 96 individuals with neurologist-confirmed epilepsy and 85 healthy controls across multiple sessions. Eight global EEG measures were evaluated: aperiodic exponent and offset, sample entropy, detrended fluctuation analysis exponent and derived index, spatial gamma-band phase consistency, and absolute and relative alpha power. Primary group inference used linear mixed-effects models to account for repeated recordings and sessions within participants. Secondary analyses examined group differences in measures temporal stability and cross-metric correlation. We examined only in epilepsy group associations between EEG-derived metrics and ASMs count, and their impact on cross-metric correlations. Results In the mixed-effects models, aperiodic offset and exponent were the only measures with FDR-robust group effects. Aperiodic offset showed higher consistency in epilepsy than in healthy controls (standardized epilepsy-minus-healthy beta = 0.52, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.78, FDR-adjusted p = 0.001). Across sessions, consistency was higher in epilepsy for aperiodic offset exponent (beta = 0.32, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.54, FDR-adjusted p = 0.018). Cross-metric correlation patterns were largely preserved between groups. Medication associations were examined separately within the epilepsy group. Higher ASM burden was associated with higher alpha relative power. Significance Among eight candidate EEG measures aperiodic offset and exponent differed between groups (epilepsy vs. healthy controls), and both were more reproducible across sessions in epilepsy. Relative alpha power tracked within-person antiseizure medication burden, suggesting that disease-related and treatment-related EEG markers may be complementary. These findings, obtained from routine clinical EEG in an open dataset, suggest aperiodic spectral parameters as candidates for prospective validation as biomarkers.
